findings.title: Live node sits exactly at the default peer cap: 21 peers, zero spare slots
Full eclipse needs all 21 slots from at least 6 IPs; at 90% address-pool share the outbound draw succeeds with probability 0.349
Peer identities are admin-only: the public cannot see who the 21 peers are, so eclipse exposure of the live node cannot be audited from outside
One public IP can hold at most 2 inbound slots (ipLimit default 2); 6 distinct IPs fill all 11 inbound slots
Peer-score latency edge is small: a 5 ms attacker wins the fetch-pack pick in 18.2% of trials against twenty 50 ms peers (fair share 4.76%)
Manifest flood amplification is bounded: at most 500 manifests and 512 KiB per batch, at most 1000 untrusted manifests per message

findings.evidence: outputs/derived/drill-results.json (drill C, cases C-02..C-03); src/test/overlay/manifest_flood_test.cpp line 238
findings.title: The 512-byte manifest cap is enforced: a 513-byte manifest is rejected, a 512-byte one accepted
Churn refill is one 10 s batch when candidates exist, but the backoff ladder (to 55 s per failed endpoint, 143 s over 10 failures) slows recovery under repeated failure
Squelch limits validation and proposal relay to a randomly selected subset of peers, concentrating relay on a few peers per round
Only protocol versions 2.1 and 2.2 are spoken; there is no downgrade path below 2.1
Send-queue pressure disconnects peers: 192 queued messages with 4 consecutive over-target intervals, plus resource charges that drop misbehaving peers
Cluster members and reserved peers bypass the slot caps entirely, so a reservation is a trust decision, not a capacity one
